analysis.body:
# Sector Analysis: Insurance

According to the Census Bureau, 40.0% of finance and insurance firms reported using AI in the prior two weeks, up from 36.8% in the prior period. This adoption sits within a sector where AI is now deployed across underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection. Per NAIC, insurers use AI-powered chatbots to answer customer questions and assist with transactions, while in claims processing AI estimates repair costs and assesses damage using photos and historical data. The technology also supports a shift from reactive "detect and repair" approaches to proactive "predict and prevent" models, where AI identifies risks earlier to help customers avoid losses.

The concentration of AI capability and investment in insurance remains tied to data-intensive functions. NAIC notes that insurers collect many types of data, and AI tools analyze this information quickly to identify patterns, manage risk, and support decision-making. Image recognition, language understanding, and large-scale analysis of unstructured text, images, and video have become practical. Large language models like ChatGPT, CoPilot, Claude, and Gemini are being adopted for document summarization and writing assistance, though NAIC cautions that these tools do not truly understand context and may generate plausible but incorrect information, requiring careful human review for important decisions.

Regulation and compliance form the operative layer. NAIC set the supervisory framework and established the Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group in 2019 to study AI development, its use in the sector, and its impact on consumer protection and privacy. NAIC developed regulatory principles adopted by the full membership at the 2020 Summer National Meeting. Starting in 2021, the Working Group began surveying insurers across lines of business—private passenger auto, homeowners, life insurance, and health insurance—issuing aggregate reports in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023, and May 2025. Insurers remain responsible for complying with insurance laws, regulations, fairness standards, and consumer protection rules, including requirements to avoid unfair discrimination. State insurance regulators oversee how AI is used in underwriting, pricing, marketing, and claims decisions and may require companies to explain these deployments.

Benchmarking and comparative assessment have emerged as tools for tracking maturity. The Evident AI Index benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across the financial services sector, providing insurers with data and research to inform investment and strategic choices. Evident publishes an AI Index for Insurance and conducts annual symposiums where senior AI leaders in the sector exchange insights on deploying AI in global financial institutions. AM Best, the insurance rating agency, evaluates innovation and digital maturity as part of its broader assessments, allowing technology capability to reach credit opinion.

Human judgment remains central to the insurance AI model. Per NAIC, AI is more likely to support human workers than replace them entirely. Actuaries, underwriters, claims professionals, agents, and customer service representatives still exercise judgment, review information, and work directly with consumers. Human oversight is described as an important part of insurance decision-making, suggesting that AI adoption in the sector is being designed as an augmentation layer rather than a wholesale displacement of professional roles. For firms considering deployment, the regulatory clarity and governance framework established by NAIC, combined with active oversight of fairness and discrimination, indicate a sector where AI investment must be paired with compliance infrastructure and human-in-the-loop processes.
